r3-p04-002: The system is built as a hardware acquisition unit and a software analysis unit. The hardware components and the reasons for each design choice are listed in the table below.
r3-p04-006: 3-axis vibration — detects changes in natural frequency and other vibration traits
r3-p04-008: Temperature/humidity — compensates for environment-driven normal variation
r3-p04-012: Runs real-time acquisition, tapper control, FFT, anomaly score and dashboard on one device
r3-p04-014: First model for structural-condition tests such as mass distribution
r3-p04-016: Low damping gives sharp resonance peaks; bolted joints give repeatable boundary conditions
r3-p04-018: Automatic excitation at fixed force, period and position — removes manual variation and narrows normal scatter
r3-p04-020: Deck surface temperature — logged as a candidate compensation input (waterproof probe, ₩4,200)
r3-p04-022: Remote access to the field node and data checks (Eduplayer ELR22, ₩59,650)
r3-p04-024: Power for installation where no mains supply exists (30,000 mAh, ₩20,900)
r3-p04-025: The core measurement and processing hardware — ADXL355Z evaluation board ₩84,589, DHT22 sensor ₩5,680 and Raspberry Pi 5 (about ₩100,000 for the 2–4 GB RAM model) — costs about ₩190,000 in total; adding the DS18B20 surface-temperature sensor (₩4,200), the LTE router (₩59,650) and the power bank (₩20,900) used in stage 3 brings it to about ₩275,000. This is far below existing SHM measurement costing tens of millions of won, which presupposes ultra-precise piezoelectric accelerometers and dedicated acquisition equipment (see 1.3 and [1]), supporting this work's goal of a low-cost configuration that can be deployed on many small and medium bridges.
r3-p04-027: The software analysis unit consists of two programs, one for acquisition and one for analysis. The acquisition program runs in Python on the Raspberry Pi and writes the ADXL355Z 3-axis acceleration at 200 Hz (500 Hz in stages 2 and 3) and the DHT22 temperature and relative humidity at about 2-second intervals to a single CSV file. The analysis program splits this file into time windows and performs, in order, FFT and feature extraction, residual calculation by multivariate regression on temperature T and relative humidity RH, standardization, reconstruction-error-based anomaly scoring, a 99th-percentile threshold decision, and band-contribution output.
r3-p04-028: In stage 2 this configuration is extended into a real-time system on a Raspberry Pi 5. The acquisition logger, tapper control and analysis server run on the same device to guarantee a shared clock; the window right after each tap (from t₀+0.05 s for 2.0 s, where t₀ is the tap time) is cut out, and its spectrum and anomaly score are computed immediately and shown on a web dashboard. The dashboard refreshes about every 0.7 s with the live z-axis waveform, tap spectrum, ratio to threshold (anomaly score ÷ threshold), peak frequency, RMS, temperature/humidity and band contributions; a ratio below 0.8 is shown as normal, 0.8–1.0 as caution, and 1.0 or above as an anomaly candidate. The real-time decision is for on-site monitoring; all raw data, including condition codes, are saved to CSV and used for model training and evaluation.
r3-p05-000: For the stage-3 real bridges, the acquisition program was changed to record ambient vibration continuously without a tapper, the DS18B20 surface temperature was added, and CSV files are split hourly for long unattended collection. Anomaly detection is not run in real time on site but in batch after collection.
r3-p05-002: On the stage-1 foam-board model, the ADXL355Z is mounted at mid-span, where the first bending response is largest (x = L/2, y = B/2 for span L and width B), and the vertical z axis, which reflects vertical bending, is the main axis of analysis.
r3-p05-003: On the stage-2 aluminum model, every position is defined along the length of the deck (overall length 600 mm) with x = 0 at the left end. The solenoid tapper strikes the centerline of the top surface at mid-span, x = 300 mm, so that every tap consistently excites the dominant mode, and the gap between tip and deck is held at 2–5 mm with a card gauge in all conditions so that they touch only at the moment of impact. The ADXL355Z is attached to the underside of the deck at x = 240 mm, away from directly below the impact point, to measure the large bending response near mid-span while avoiding the local impact component right after the tap and interference from the weights and the impact point on top. Weights are placed at x = 150 mm (L/4) and x = 450 mm (3L/4), the same proportions as in stage 1 (Figure 1).
r3-p05-004: In both experiments the DHT22 and the Raspberry Pi are kept off the vibrating structure (deck and piers) so that they do not affect the bridge's mass or stiffness. In stage 1 they were placed beside the model with the cables fixed loosely; in stage 2 the DHT22 is fixed on the base rail at x = 400 mm so that temperature and relative humidity around the bridge are recorded at the same position in every condition, and the Raspberry Pi sits beside the base, away from the deck, so that cable tension and mass do not influence the vibration response.

r3-p05-007: 1. Vibration and temperature/humidity acquisition: 3-axis acceleration is collected from the ADXL355Z, and temperature T and relative humidity RH from the DHT22. The actual natural-frequency range was checked in a preliminary test so that the analysis band stays within the Nyquist limit, and the plan was to raise the sampling rate to 500 Hz if the measured fundamental approached or exceeded the 100 Hz Nyquist limit of 200 Hz sampling. On the stage-2 aluminum model, preliminary measurement after assembly showed the dominant-mode frequency above that limit, so the sampling rate was fixed at 500 Hz and the measurement range at ±8 g (measured natural frequencies are given in 3.4). Excitation is by manual tapping in stage 1 and, in stage 2,
r3-p06-000: by automatic taps from the solenoid auto-tapper (at a fixed period after warm-up); tap times are logged on the same clock, and only the free-vibration segment right after each tap is used as the unit of analysis.
r3-p06-001: 2. Signal preprocessing and frequency-band feature extraction: the DC offset is removed from the acceleration signal and the spectrum is estimated (FFT/STFT in stage 1; in stage 2 the Welch method, which reduces noise by averaging spectra over short segments). RMS, standard deviation, peak-to-peak, peak frequency and power, band energies and so on are computed per segment and axis; the analysis bands are reset to match the measured dominant peak, and from stage 2 onward eight z-axis features are used, with amplitude and energy log-scaled and band energies normalized as ratios (bands and features are listed in 3.2). Temperature T and relative humidity RH are used for environmental compensation. The z-axis peak frequency serves as the indicator of the dominant-mode natural frequency, and the band-wise analysis is an auxiliary indicator that explains which vibration characteristic departed from the baseline, not a way to locate damage.
r3-p06-002: 3. Multivariate regression compensation of the normal natural frequency by temperature and humidity: on normal data, a multivariate regression that predicts the natural frequency from temperature T and relative humidity RH is learned; at inference, the difference between the measurement f and the prediction f̂ = g(T, RH), r = f − f̂, is defined as the residual corrected for the temperature/humidity effect. The same regression and residual calculation are applied to every vibration feature, and the resulting residual features are the input to the anomaly-detection model. Because the residual can still contain sensor noise, mounting condition and operational loading besides structural anomaly candidates, it is used as a criterion for detecting anomaly candidates, not as a confirmation of damage.
r3-p06-003: 4. Unsupervised anomaly detection with an Autoencoder: the Autoencoder is trained only on standardized residual features from the normal state (architecture in Figure 2). The model compresses the input into a low-dimensional latent representation and reconstructs it, learning only the correlation structure of normal data, so data that depart from the normal pattern have a larger reconstruction error. The threshold is set at the 99th percentile of the reconstruction error on normal validation data (in stage 2, the error distribution of 90 normal windows held out exclusively for the threshold; see 3.2). Because both training and thresholding use only normal data, operation can begin without any damage data. The stage-1 implementation used the PCA reconstruction error, equivalent to a linear Autoencoder; stage 2 adopted a nonlinear Autoencoder with an 8–3–8 hidden structure (tanh, early stopping).
r3-p06-005: 5. Band-wise reconstruction-error contribution: when an anomaly is detected, the system also analyzes which frequency bands (or bands around modes) have large reconstruction errors. A contribution is computed as “that feature's reconstruction error ÷ total reconstruction error.”
r3-p06-006: 6. Output and precision-inspection alerts: when the anomaly score exceeds the threshold, the system raises an alarm and outputs the anomaly score, a before/after comparison of temperature/humidity compensation, the main contributing bands, the rate of change in natural frequency, the band contributions and an interpretation for inspectors.
